title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether adding a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. Under preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial LLM generation per task reused across the paired arms), we ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial). Declared model: gpt-5-mini; validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5; repair budget: ≤1 repair per guarded task. Execution completed as planned (planned episodes = 480, completed = 480, hosted_model_call_event_count = 240, model_calls_used = 240). Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms: baseline = 240/240 safe (unsafe_apply = 0), guarded = 240/240 safe (unsafe_apply = 0). The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. No validator‑triggered repairs were applied because the shared initial candidate passed deterministic validation in every task. We make explicit that, under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics, the paired contrast can only differ when the shared initial candidate fails validation or when a validator‑triggered repair is applied. We report the preregistered design, complete execution accounting, artifact‑grounded analysis, and an evidence‑based failure analysis that explains the null paired outcome and provides concrete recommendations for informative future GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction:
High‑level operator intent is increasingly translated to device configurations by generative models and agentic workflows. Execution‑grounded evaluation—where generated configurations are applied to emulated device images and deterministically scored—reveals workflow and ordering faults that token‑level metrics miss [1]. A commonly proposed mitigation is generate–validate–repair (GVR): the model emits a candidate configuration, a deterministic verifier checks workflow and semantic invariants, and an automated repair routine rewrites the candidate when violations are detected [2,3].

This paper reports a fully preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation that asked a single, precise estimand: does integrating a deterministic verifier (with at most one validator‑triggered repair) reduce the rate of unsafe configuration application relative to an LLM‑only pipeline? We implemented a paired design with shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial LLM generation per task reused by both arms) and executed the registered adapter to completion. Our contributions are (1) a preregistered experimental run and full execution accounting (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01); (2) artifact‑grounded reporting of exact per‑call traces, validator traces, and analysis artifacts that map to the preregistered estimand; and (3) a failure analysis that explains a null paired outcome and gives artifact‑supported recommendations for future, informative paired GVR studies.
sections.related_work: Evaluation and benchmark work has argued for executable, closed‑loop tests for agentic NetOps to surface planning and workflow faults not visible in text‑only tasks [1]. Prior configuration‑repair systems and automatic program‑repair literature document generate–validate or generate–validate–repair patterns and show that validators enable high syntactic repair coverage on many benchmarked misconfigurations [2,4]. Survey and position papers discuss tool augmentation, verifier integration, and uncertainty calibration as architectural patterns for agentic systems and highlight open empirical questions under distribution shift and adversarial probes [3,5]. Practical emulation benchmarks (e.g., NetConfArena) and configuration analyzers (Batfish evolution) provide precedent and motivate our closed‑loop design [1,6]. Our study situates itself among these works by performing a preregistered paired test of a canonical GVR pipeline in an emulation‑grounded environment and by archiving all artifacts for reproducibility.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0d...). The primary estimand is the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline = (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate), where unsafe_apply = 1 and safe_apply = 0. The archived execution outputs report 'success' as the safe outcome; we explicitly map archived names to the preregistered estimand in this paper: archived baseline_success_count = 240 corresponds to baseline safe_apply = 240 (baseline unsafe_apply = 0).

Design and sampling: N = 240 distinct tasks executed as paired episodes (baseline LLM‑only vs guarded GVR) with the following composition: in‑distribution 60% (144), distribution‑shift 20% (48), adversarial‑prompt 20% (48). Tasks were deterministically generated by the benchmark task generator deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and blocked into topology/vendor clusters per the preregistration.

Generation semantics and adapter contract: Execution used the registered adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1 under shared_initial_candidate semantics: exactly one initial LLM generation was produced per task and reused for both arms. The guarded arm could invoke up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. This contract is preregistered and materially constrains estimand interpretation: a paired divergence is possible only if the shared initial candidate fails validation or a repair is applied.

Model and validator: Declared model version: "gpt-5-mini" (execution/model_configuration.json). The deterministic verifier was deterministic_netops_validator_v5; validator checks and scoring rules are recorded in archived validator traces (execution/scoring/*.json). Repair budget per guarded task: at most one repair call.

Runtime budget, retries, and exclusions: Planned_episode_count = 480; maximum_model_calls = 480. Runtime sampling parameters were recorded for each call. Retry policy permitted up to two infra‑recovery attempts; unrecoverable infra failures were to be marked as infra‑failed and excluded from the primary analysis per preregistration; no such exclusions occurred in this run.

Scoring and analysis: Each final configuration was deterministically scored safe (0) or unsafe (1) by the validator and emulator oracle. Analysis used the registered paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor. Primary analysis produced the paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv), a bootstrap 95% percentile CI computed with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729), and an exact two‑sided McNemar test on discordant pairs. Predeclared sensitivity analyses include treating infra failures as unsafe and including possible 'false‑safe' flags; none were needed because no such cases occurred.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The adapter completed execution per the preregistration: planned_episode_count = 480, completed_episode_count = 480, complete_pair_count = 240. Hosted_model_call_event_count = 240 and model_calls_used = 240 (execution_manifest). No infra failures, no unscorable episodes, and no preregistered exclusions occurred (analysis/missingness_summary.csv).

Primary binary outcomes: All episodes were scored safe under both arms. Condition summary (analysis/condition_summary.csv): baseline successes = 240, baseline failures = 0 (baseline unsafe_apply = 0); guarded successes = 240, guarded failures = 0 (guarded unsafe_apply = 0). Paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv): n11 (both safe) = 240; n10 = 0; n01 = 0; n00 = 0. The paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00. Bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (resamples = 10,000; seed = 1729; analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The analysis artifacts (analysis/results.json and CSVs) are archived and referenced in the execution manifest.

Validator and repair activity: No validator‑triggered repairs were applied (repair_attempts = 0 across archived repair logs). Representative per‑task validator traces (e.g., execution/scoring/task-000004-guarded.json) show validator validation_before and validation_after metadata (difficulty pattern, required_command_count, normalized_configuration) and record validator PASS semantics and the lack of repair prompts. Because the guarded final configuration equaled the shared initial candidate in every episode, baseline and guarded outcomes were identical for every pair.

Reconciliation and audit: Deterministic reconciliation artifacts confirm consistent accounting (deterministic_reconciliation.json: all_deterministic_consistency_checks_passed = true). Provider call audit recorded exactly one shared_initial_generation per task (provider_call_audit.hosted_model_call_event_count = 240). Contamination checks and planned adversary tagging produced no cross‑condition leaks (analysis/contamination_summary.csv empty).
sections.discussion:
Why a null paired outcome occurred: Two preregistered execution facts explain the degenerate paired contrast. First, shared_initial_candidate semantics produced one LLM output per task reused by both arms; second, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 passed that candidate in every task. Under these conditions the guarded arm had no opportunity to apply repairs or alter outcomes, so no discordant pairs could arise and the paired estimate collapsed to zero with a degenerate bootstrap CI and McNemar p = 1.0. This outcome is consistent with the preregistered estimand and was faithfully reported by the registered analysis executor.

Design implications and recommendations (artifact‑grounded): Based on archived traces and analysis, we recommend the following to obtain informative paired contrasts in future runs: (A) permit independent initial generations per arm (remove shared_initial_candidate semantics) or introduce controlled generator perturbations so validators have opportunities to flag failures; (B) increase repair budget and permit iterative/multi‑attempt repairs so the repair routine can be exercised when validator failures occur; (C) strengthen adversary sampling beyond a single fixed attacker seed to probe adaptive prompt injections; (D) broaden deterministic verifier semantic coverage and instrument cross‑checks between validator PASS and emulator outcomes to detect potential false‑safe cases. Each recommendation maps directly to archived artifacts: the provider_call_audit and per‑task validator traces show that no repairs were triggered and that shared initial outputs were identical across arms (execution/responses/*.txt and execution/scoring/*.json).

Threats to validity: Internal validity is constrained by the shared_initial_candidate semantics and a single tested model (gpt‑5‑mini). Construct validity is limited by the finite rule coverage of deterministic_netops_validator_v5; unmodeled semantic fault classes may exist. External validity is limited by the synthetic NetConfArena‑style corpus and emulated devices (not production multi‑vendor deployments). Conclusion validity: baseline unsafe rate = 0 prevents detecting verifier benefit; future designs should anticipate generator variability or stronger adversaries to produce informative discordant pairs. All these threats are traceable to archived execution artifacts and are reported here to bound inference.
sections.conclusion:
We executed a fully preregistered paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a GVR pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration. Observed outcome: every paired episode was safe under both arms, yielding paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). Crucially, under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the guarded arm can only affect paired outcomes when the single shared initial candidate fails deterministic validation or when a validator‑triggered repair is applied; in this run the validator passed every shared initial candidate and no repairs were invoked. We archive the preregistration, per‑call traces, validator traces, and analysis artifacts so follow‑up experiments can vary generation semantics, adversary strength, or verifier coverage. Future paired studies seeking to estimate verifier benefit empirically should permit generator variability between arms or expand repair/search budgets to produce informative discordant pairs.

disclosure_statement: Models and orchestration: Execution used a single hosted model (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini") via the registered adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1. The guarded pipeline used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. Runtime sampling: execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null (unset); unset temperature does not imply determinism by the hosted provider and sampling nondeterminism remains possible; all model‑call metadata were archived. Preregistration and autonomy: the study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0dc935a8754bf2dfbe6869ff989c47f1db0d93e2ca34809be8ebf95e26) and executed under the frozen plan after the autonomy lock; a human Research Director selected the broad topic family and constrained the initial master prompt prior to the lock; no manual human editing of the technical manuscript content occurred post‑lock. Preregistered generation semantics: the registered adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial generation per task reused across both arms), so only validator‑triggered repairs (or validator failures of the shared candidate) could create paired divergences; this constraint is explicitly reported in Methods, Results, Abstract, and Conclusion. Execution accounting (archived): planned_episode_count = 480, completed_episode_count = 480, complete_pair_count = 240, hosted_model_call_event_count = 240, model_calls_used = 240. Immutable master prompt: the initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Reproducibility pointer: archived execution manifest, per‑call traces, task manifests, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are included in the execution bundle (execution/execution_manifest.json and analysis/). Human role and autonomy boundary: prior to the autonomy lock the human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial prompt; all literature search, experiment selection, preregistration, execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting occurred autonomously after the lock per the track rules.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across models, prompts, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.

Verifier coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite set of checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected by the verifier, and verifier PASS vs simulator outcome mismatches were planned to be flagged and analyzed (none occurred in this run).
